title: Python 3.14 subinterpreters cut a GIL bottleneck from 3.6s to 0.9s
excerpt: Four subinterpreters finished a CPU-bound prime count in 0.9 seconds, while four threads needed 3.6 seconds.
body:
A CPU-bound job that counts primes below 400 000 ran in 3.6 seconds when split across four regular threads on a four-core machine. The same workload distributed over four new subinterpreters in Python 3.14 finished in about 0.9 seconds, essentially the time a single thread needs for a quarter of the work. The author of the experiment expected the subinterpreters to behave like classic threads when sharing a GIL, but a single interpreter outright rejected a second concurrent call.

## Subinterpreters give each interpreter its own GIL  

Python 3.14 introduced the concurrent.interpreters module, the first standard-library entry point that lets pure Python code create subinterpreters without writing C extensions. The feature is based on PEP 734, which builds on a C-API capability that has existed since Python 1.5.

The key promise is that each subinterpreter receives its own Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). Because the GIL is what normally serialises bytecode execution, giving every interpreter a separate lock should allow true CPU-bound parallelism on multiple cores, without falling back to the multiprocessing module.

## Real parallelism shown by a prime-count benchmark  

The benchmark used a straightforward double loop that tests every integer below 400 000 for primality. No external libraries or C extensions were involved, so the GIL is the only contention point. Running the workload in a single thread took roughly 0.8 seconds. When four threads attempted the same four units of work, the total rose to 3.6 seconds, a little worse than the 3.2 seconds you would expect from perfect serialisation because the GIL forces frequent context switches.

Creating four subinterpreters and assigning each unit of work to its own interpreter reduced the elapsed time to about 0.9 seconds. The extra three units of work added almost no overhead, matching the single-thread baseline. This speed-up mirrors what multiprocessing achieves, confirming that the separate GILs provide genuine parallel execution rather than a scheduling illusion.

## A single interpreter rejects concurrent threads  

The PEP’s headline claim is that each interpreter has its own GIL, so the author tried to run two threads against the same subinterpreter. Classic Python would let both threads run, taking turns on the shared GIL. Instead, the subinterpreter raised an immediate error:

```
Exception in thread Thread-2 (_call):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/concurrent/interpreters/__init__.py", line 226, in _call
    res, excinfo = _interpreters.call(self._id, callable, args, kwargs, restrict=True)
concurrent.interpreters.InterpreterError: interpreter already running
```

The documentation states that `interpreters.create()` returns an “idle” interpreter, and the observed behavior confirms that an interpreter is either idle or running, with no intermediate state. If more than one task needs to run concurrently, the correct pattern is to create a separate interpreter for each task. A thread pool that targets a single shared interpreter, the pattern shown in typical `ThreadPoolExecutor` tutorials, does not translate; it yields one interpreter’s worth of work and an exception rather than graceful queuing.

## Startup cost is higher than a process pool  

Another common assumption is that subinterpreters are cheaper to start than full OS processes because they avoid duplicating the entire address space. The author measured the time to spin up four workers, each receiving a 200 000-element list as initial state. The creation and warm-up phase took roughly twice as long as launching four processes via the classic fork-based pool, and it was also slower than the newer forkserver default.

The extra setup time was about 80 milliseconds per interpreter, which the 0.9-second benchmark easily dwarfed. Nevertheless, the data show that “subinterpreters are lighter than processes” does not hold at creation time; the benefit, if any, lies in avoiding a full process fork rather than in faster startup.

## The takeaway  

Subinterpreters in Python 3.14 provide a separate GIL per interpreter, delivering near-linear speed-up for CPU-bound work across cores. However, an interpreter accepts only one concurrent caller; to run multiple tasks in parallel you must create multiple interpreters. The startup cost is comparable to, or higher than, spawning processes, so the primary advantage is avoiding a full address-space copy rather than faster initialization. Use a pool of subinterpreters when you need true parallelism, but treat each interpreter as a single-threaded worker.

sources.title: Python 3.14's concurrent.interpreters module turns a 3.6-second GIL bottleneck into 0.9 seconds
